chapter.name: Union and Its Territory
chapter.blurb: Articles 1 to 4, reorganisation of states, evolution of states and union territories.

scope_in.item: Evolution of states and union territories

concepts.name: Union of States and the territory of India (Articles 1 and 2)
concepts.description: The name and type of polity, the three categories of territory and Parliament's power to admit or establish states.
concepts.idea: Article 1 calls India a Union of States, and Article 2 lets Parliament admit or establish new states.
concepts.rule: Article 1 says 'India, that is, Bharat, shall be a Union of States'. It deals with the name of the country and its type of polity. The Assembly could not agree on a single name, so it used both the traditional Bharat and the modern India. Ambedkar explained that 'Union' was preferred to 'Federation' for two reasons: the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the states, and the states have no right to secede; it is indestructible and divided into states only for administrative convenience. The territory of India has three categories: territories of the states, union territories, and territories that may be acquired. The First Schedule names the states and union territories; at present there are 28 states and 8 union territories. 'Territory of India' is wider than 'Union of India', which includes only states. States share powers with the Centre, while union territories and acquired territories are administered directly by the Centre. India can acquire territory by cession, occupation, conquest or subjugation, as with Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Goa, Daman and Diu, Puducherry and Sikkim. Article 2 lets Parliament admit into the Union or establish new states on terms it thinks fit; it concerns states not already in the Union.
concepts.example: Special provisions in Part XXI apply to states such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam and Sikkim.

concepts.name: Parliament's power to reorganise states (Articles 3 and 4) and the Berubari case
concepts.description: How Parliament forms new states, the conditions, why states are 'destructible', and the limits on ceding territory.
concepts.idea: Parliament can form, alter or rename states under Article 3 by simple majority after referring to the state legislature.
concepts.rule: Article 3 authorises Parliament to form a new state by separating territory, or by uniting states or parts of states; increase or diminish the area of a state; alter its boundaries; and alter its name. Two conditions apply: the bill can be introduced only with the President's prior recommendation, and the President must refer it to the state legislature for its views within a specified time. Neither is bound by the state's views, and a fresh reference is not needed for each amendment. For a union territory no reference to its legislature is needed. So the Constitution guarantees no state's existence, and India is 'an indestructible union of destructible states', unlike the USA, an indestructible union of indestructible states. Article 4 says such laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not amendments under Article 368 and can be passed by simple majority. In the Berubari reference (1960) the Supreme Court held that Article 3 does not permit ceding Indian territory to a foreign country, so it required a constitutional amendment, which became the 9th Amendment (1960). In 1969 the Court held that settling a boundary dispute needs only executive action, not an amendment.
concepts.example: A law forming a new state is passed by a simple majority and is not treated as a constitutional amendment.

concepts.name: Exchange of territories with Bangladesh (100th Amendment)
concepts.description: The 2015 deal on enclaves and the background of border disputes.
concepts.idea: The 100th Amendment (2015) gave effect to an exchange of enclaves and settlement of the border with Bangladesh.
concepts.rule: The 100th Amendment Act (2015) gave effect to the agreement and protocol with Bangladesh: India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh and Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India, with transfer of adverse possessions and demarcation of a 6.1 km undemarcated border stretch. It modified the First Schedule for four states: Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura. The India-Bangladesh land boundary is about 4096.7 km. It was fixed by the Radcliffe Award of 1947; disputes were addressed by the Bagge Award of 1950 and the Nehru-Noon Agreement of 1958, and the division of Berubari was challenged in the Supreme Court, leading to the 9th Amendment (1960), which could not be notified for former East Pakistan. The Land Boundary Agreement of 16 May 1974 was not ratified because it involved transfer of territory requiring an amendment. A Protocol signed on 6 September 2011 resolved the issues.
concepts.example: The 2011 Protocol forms an integral part of the Land Boundary Agreement of 1974.

concepts.name: Integration of princely states and the 1950 classification of states
concepts.description: The options given to princely states and the Part A, B, C and D scheme of 1950.
concepts.idea: Most princely states joined India in 1947 and the 1950 Constitution grouped units into four parts.
concepts.rule: At independence India had British provinces and princely states under British paramountcy. The Indian Independence Act (1947) created two dominions and gave princely states three options: join India, join Pakistan or stay independent. Of 552 states within India's geographical boundaries, 549 joined India, and the other three, Hyderabad, Junagarh and Kashmir, were integrated later: Hyderabad by police action, Junagarh by referendum and Kashmir by the Instrument of Accession. In 1950 the Constitution classified units into Part A states (nine former governor's provinces), Part B states (nine former princely states with legislatures), Part C states (ten, former chief commissioners' provinces and some princely states, centrally administered) and Part D (the Andaman and Nicobar Islands), 29 in all.
concepts.example: Part D consisted only of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

concepts.name: Dhar Commission, JVP Committee, Fazl Ali Commission and the 1956 reorganisation
concepts.description: How the demand for linguistic states led to the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
concepts.idea: The demand for linguistic states led from the Dhar Commission to the Fazl Ali Commission and the 1956 Act.
concepts.rule: In June 1948 the Government appointed the Linguistic Provinces Commission under S.K. Dhar. It reported in December 1948 that states should be reorganised on administrative convenience rather than language, which caused resentment. The Congress appointed the Linguistic Provinces Committee of Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya (the JVP Committee) in December 1948; in April 1949 it rejected language as the basis. In October 1953 Andhra state, the first linguistic state, was created from the Telugu-speaking areas of Madras after a long agitation and the death of Potti Sriramulu following a 56-day fast. The States Reorganisation Commission of December 1953, headed by Fazl Ali with K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru, reported in September 1955, accepted language broadly but rejected 'one language, one state', giving four factors: unity and security, linguistic and cultural homogeneity, financial, economic and administrative considerations, and welfare planning. It suggested abolishing the four-fold classification and creating 16 states and 3 centrally administered territories. The States Reorganisation Act and the 7th Amendment (1956) created 14 states and 6 union territories from 1 November 1956; Part C states were abolished and Kerala was formed by merging Travancore-Cochin, Malabar and Kasaragod.
concepts.example: The Fazl Ali Commission's other two members were K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.

concepts.name: New states and union territories after 1956
concepts.description: States created since 1956, and the special cases of Sikkim, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Jammu and Kashmir.
concepts.idea: The map of India has kept changing since 1956, from Gujarat in 1960 to Telangana in 2014 and the Union Territories of 2019.
concepts.rule: In 1960 Bombay was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat, the 15th state. Dadra and Nagar Haveli, liberated from Portuguese rule in 1954, became a union territory by the 10th Amendment (1961); Goa, Daman and Diu were acquired by police action in 1961 and became a union territory by the 12th Amendment (1962), with Goa becoming a state in 1987. Puducherry, handed over by the French in 1954, became a union territory by the 14th Amendment (1962). Nagaland became the 16th state in 1963. In 1966 Punjab was divided into Haryana (17th state) and the union territory of Chandigarh; Himachal Pradesh became the 18th state in 1971. In 1972 Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya became the 19th, 20th and 21st states, with Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh as union territories. Sikkim became an associate state by the 35th Amendment (1974, Article 2A) and a full state, the 22nd, by the 36th Amendment (1975) after a referendum. In 1987 Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa became the 23rd, 24th and 25th states. In 2000 Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand became the 26th, 27th and 28th, and in 2014 Telangana the 29th. Andhra state (1953, capital Kurnool) grew into Andhra Pradesh in 1956; the 2014 Act bifurcated it. In 2019 Article 370's special status for Jammu and Kashmir ended and it was split into the UTs of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. Dadra and Nagar Haveli merged with Daman and Diu in 2020.
concepts.example: In 2020 the UTs of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were merged into one.
